newsitem.title: UK: Chronology of UK Conservatives' inflation record.
newsitem.headline: Chronology of UK Conservatives' inflation record.

text.p: Following is a brief chronology of the Britain's ruling Conservatives record on inflation.
Official figures out on Thursday showed underlying inflation rose 2.7 percent in the year to March, the lowest rate of increase since May 1995 --
May 1979 - Conservatives win power and inherit inflation of around 10.6 percent and interest rates of 12.0 percent.

Summer 1979 - Government immediately almost doubles Value Added Tax and raises interest rates, pushing inflation higher. Upward pressure also comes from spiralling oil prices and wages as Tories honour election commitment to award generous public sector pay increases. Average inflation rate for the year rises to 13.4 percent.
1980 - Economy heads into recession but inflation surges higher as full effect of VAT, wage rises hit home. Average rate 18.0 percent. Base rates start to fall.
1981 - Economy starts to come out of recession, further easing in monetary policy. Inflation falls to average of 11.9 percent.
1982-1986 - Steady economic recovery but inflation continues to fall, helped by lower oil prices and impact of labour market reforms which reduce wage pressures. Average for 1986 -- 3.4 percent.

1987 - Exchange rate assumes increasingly important role in monetary policy considerations as becomes clear money supply aggregates, which the Conservative government had tailored policy to, are misleading.
1988 - Economic growth accelerates sharply and inflation picks up, flamed by financial deregulation and housing market boom. Inflation averages 4.9 percent.
1989 - Prices pick up strongly to average of 7.8 percent in year. Interest rates rise to 15 percent to slow growth and reduce price pressures.
1990 - Economy enters recession late in the year, but inflation continues to climb to average of 9.5 percent. Pound joins Exchange Rate Mechanism in October at 2.95 marks central rate.
1991 - Inflation falls to average of 5.9 percent as recession bites.

1992 - Pound ejected from ERM, but despite sudden and massive devaluation, inflation continues to fall. New monetary framework established with explicit inflation target -- 2.5 percent for underlying rate by the end of the Parliament -- monthly monetary meetings and quarterly Bank of England reports.
1993 - Inflation hits lowest level for 30 years of 1.2 percent as interest rates fall (underlying inflation higher at almost 3.0 pct).

1994 - Interest rates raised pre-emptively by 50 basis points to 5.75 percent. Taken as sign from Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke that he will be tough on inflation which averages 2.4 percent in year.
1995 - Inflation heads higher to 3.5 percent as economy recovers.
April 1997 - March underlying inflation falls to 2.7 percent in month before election. Government narrowly misses its 2.5 percent target.
